# 2026-11-22: A mechanical bit {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
**Status:** promoted to @sec-bit · **Thread:** T7 · **Checked by:** `tests/test_bistable.py`
:::

**Question.** Everything in the book so far is linear. Computation needs memory: a body
has to keep a record of something the environment did, long after it happened. How long
can a body hold a record of a single event, such as whether it was pushed, against its own
thermal noise? And what does a stretch of the body's history hold about that event?

**Findings.**

- *A linear body forgets on its relaxation time.* A push leaves the body displaced, the
    displacement relaxes, and the record is gone after a few relaxation times. A larger
    push only buys time logarithmically.
- *A barrier keeps the record exponentially longer.* An element with two wells keeps
    which well it is in until thermal noise carries it over the barrier, which takes a
    time that grows like $e^{\Delta E/\sigma_T^2}$. With the barrier at 10 times the thermal
    energy, the bit lasts about 1,000 times longer than the same push in a harmonic
    element.
- *History and state agree.* For a body whose future depends only on its present state, a
    window of its history holds exactly what the state at the start of the window holds
    about a past event. The information can only fall as the window moves later. So the
    history view of the book and the idea of memory fit together: memory is the state
    carrying the past forward.

**Where it lives now.** The definitions, proofs, figures and numbers moved to @sec-bit of
the chapter on memory in mechanisms. This note keeps the dated record of the question and
what was found.
